subject: Computer Networking
title: OAuth and Web Authentication
description: Learn OAuth and Web Authentication in one minute.

hook.text: 'Sign in with Google' is everywhere. OAuth lets you log in to apps without sharing your password.

buildup.text: OAuth redirects you to the identity provider. You log in there. It sends a token back to the app.

discovery.text: The app gets an access token, not your password. The token grants limited permissions for a limited time.

twist.text: OAuth is for authorization, not authentication. OpenID Connect adds identity on top. They're often confused.

climax.text: JWTs carry claims in a signed token. The server verifies the signature without calling the identity provider.

punchline.text: OAuth delegates login. Your password stays with the provider you trust.

quiz.question: What does an app receive from OAuth instead of the user's password?
options: A time-limited access token with specific permissions
A copy of the user's password hash
Full access to the user's identity provider account

details.summary: OAuth 2.0 enables secure delegated authorization where users grant third-party applications limited access to their accounts without sharing passwords. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer for authentication. Together they power sign-in-with-Google, social logins, and API access across the web.
details.whyItMatters: OAuth and OIDC are the security foundation of the connected web. Every social login, API integration, and third-party app authorization relies on these protocols.
takeaways: OAuth grants limited access tokens instead of sharing passwords
OpenID Connect adds authentication to OAuth's authorization framework
Scopes restrict what permissions applications receive

faq.question: What is the OAuth authorization code flow?
faq.answer: The user clicks login, the app redirects to the authorization server, the user authenticates and consents, the server redirects back with a short-lived code, the app exchanges this code for access and refresh tokens server-side. This flow keeps tokens off the browser for better security.

faq.question: What are the risks of OAuth?
faq.answer: Misconfigured redirect URIs can leak tokens. Overly broad scopes grant more access than needed. Token theft enables account takeover. CSRF attacks can trick users into linking attacker accounts. PKCE extension mitigates several attacks for public clients like mobile and SPA applications.
